title: Question 8
stem:
A student designs a circuit incorporating an operational amplifier (op-amp) as shown in Fig. 8.1.

{{figure:figure_8_1}}

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: On Fig. 8.1, draw a circle around the output device.
hints: Hint 1: Think about the flow of information - which components sense the environment and which components show something to the user?
parts.proper_answer: Circle around both LEDs (B and G) on the right of the output.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot the Input, Process and Output**
Think of any sensing circuit in three blocks. Inputs sense the world, here component C (thermistor) and the variable resistor. Processing decides, here the op-amp comparator. Outputs show the result to the user.

Step 2: **Identify the LEDs**
The two LEDs labelled B (blue) and G (green) give light out to show the state of the circuit. They are both output devices, so circle around both of them.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: State the purpose of this circuit.

markscheme_points.text: indicates (whether) temperature (is) above or below a set value

hints: Hint 1: Look at what changes the input voltages - component C has the thermistor symbol, so what physical quantity must it be sensing?
Hint 2: The op-amp has two different LEDs on its output, only one can be on at a time - what kind of yes/no decision about temperature would that show?
parts.proper_answer: To indicate whether temperature is above or below a preset set value by lighting the blue or green LED.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Does Component C Do?**
Component C is a thermistor whose resistance changes with temperature. It forms a potential divider with $R_V$ to give a temperature-dependent voltage to the $+$ input of the op-amp.

Step 2: **Comparator Plus Two Colours**
The op-amp is used open-loop as a comparator. It compares the thermistor divider voltage with a fixed $3\text{ V}$ reference from X and Y. Its output saturates positive or negative, lighting either the blue LED or the green LED. So the whole circuit is a temperature comparator indicator showing if temperature is high or low relative to the set point.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem: The resistors X and Y each have resistance $R$. When conducting, the LED labelled B emits blue light and the LED labelled G emits green light.
parts.text: State whether blue light or green light is emitted when the resistance of component C is greater than the resistance $R_V$ of the variable resistor. Explain your answer.

markscheme_points.text: (when resistance of C > R_V) V^- > V^+ or V^+ < 3 V or p.d. across R_V < p.d. across R/Y/3V or p.d. across C > p.d. across R/X/3V

hints: Hint 1: Start with the two potential dividers - with X = Y, what is $V^-$? How does a large C affect the share of 6 V across $R_V$ and hence $V^+$?
Hint 2: Recall the comparator rule comparing $V^+$ and $V^-$ to decide if the output saturates to about +5 V or -5 V.
Hint 3: Think about which LED direction allows current to flow for a negative output voltage compared to 0 V ground.
parts.proper_answer: Green light is emitted. $V^- = 3\text{ V}$ and $V^+ < 3\text{ V}$, so $V^- > V^+$. Op-amp output saturates negative. Green LED is forward biased and conducts, blue LED is reverse biased and off.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the Two Input Voltages**
The left divider X and Y are equal, so: $$V^- = \frac{R}{R+R} \times 6\text{ V} = 3.0\text{ V}$$ The right divider is C on top and $R_V$ at the bottom to earth, so: $$V^+ = \frac{R_V}{R_C + R_V} \times 6\text{ V}$$ If $R_C > R_V$, most of the 6 V drops across C and only a small p.d. is left across $R_V$. So $V^+ < 3\text{ V}$. Hence $V^- > V^+$.

Step 2: **Apply the Comparator Rule**
You can remember it simply: if $V^+ > V^-$ output goes high to near $+5\text{ V}$, if $V^- > V^+$ output goes low to near $-5\text{ V}$. Here $V^-$ wins, so the output saturates negative.

Step 3: **Which LED Can Conduct?**
The bottom of both LEDs is at $0\text{ V}$ (earth). The top is at about $-5\text{ V}$. Current can only flow from $0\text{ V}$ down to $-5\text{ V}$, i.e. upwards through the LED. The green LED G is connected in that forward direction, so it conducts and emits green light. The blue LED B is reverse biased, so it stays off. Only green is on.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: State and explain what is observed as the resistance of component C is reduced.

markscheme_points.text: resistance of C becomes less than R_V or V^- < V^+

hints: Hint 1: If C gets smaller, what happens to its share of the 6 V and to the voltage $V^+$ across $R_V$?
Hint 2: At some point $V^+$ will cross the fixed 3 V level - how does that change the sign of $V^+ - V^-$ and the output polarity?
Hint 3: Link the new positive output to forward and reverse bias of the two oppositely connected LEDs.
parts.proper_answer: Resistance of C falls until $R_C < R_V$, so $V^+ > V^-$. Output saturates positive. Green LED goes out (reverse biased) and blue LED comes on (forward biased).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **$V^+$ Rises as C Falls**
Reducing $R_C$ reduces the p.d. across C and increases the p.d. across $R_V$. From $$V^+ = \frac{R_V}{R_C + R_V} \times 6\text{ V}$$ $V^+$ increases. Eventually $R_C$ becomes less than $R_V$ and $V^+$ rises above the $3\text{ V}$ reference, so $V^+ > V^-$.

Step 2: **Output Switches Polarity**
The comparator now flips to positive saturation, near $+5\text{ V}$. This is the key switching action - a small change in divider voltage causes a large swing in output.

Step 3: **LEDs Swap Over**
Now the top of the LEDs is at $+5\text{ V}$ and the bottom at $0\text{ V}$, so current can only flow downwards. The blue LED B is forward in this direction, so it turns on and emits blue light. The green LED G is now reverse biased, so the green light goes out.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Suggest the function of the variable resistor.

markscheme_points.text: changes/determines temperature at which LEDs switch

hints: Hint 1: Think about what sets the value of $V^+$ needed to equal 3 V - which component can you adjust?
parts.proper_answer: To adjust the value of $R_V$ and hence set the temperature at which the LEDs switch over.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Setting the Trip Point**
Switching happens when $R_C = R_V$, because then $V^+ = 3\text{ V} = V^-$. By changing $R_V$ you change the resistance value of the thermistor (and therefore the temperature) at which this equality occurs. So $R_V$ calibrates the threshold temperature.
